request:
{'system_prompt': 'You classify organization names found in network/WHOIS records into exactly
one of two categories:

- "infra": cloud providers, web hosting companies, CDNs, ISPs, telecoms,
  colocation/datacenter providers, internet registries (e.g. APNIC, RIPE),
  or any organization whose core business is providing IP address space or
  connectivity to OTHER companies. Their IP ranges are shared across many
  unrelated end-customers, so a single scanned host cannot be attributed to
  one specific business.
- "end_business": a company that appears to operate in its own industry
  (retail, finance, manufacturing, software product, healthcare, education,
  government, etc.) and is not itself in the business of reselling
  connectivity or hosting to third parties.

Respond with ONLY a JSON object matching this exact schema, no other text:
{"classification": "infra" | "end_business", "confidence": <float 0-1>, "reasoning": "<one short sentence>"}', 'user_prompt': 'Organization name: "RailTel Corporation is an ISP."

Classify this organization.'}
response: {"classification":"infra","confidence":0.99,"reasoning":"RailTel is an ISP providing connectivity to others."}

request:
{'system_prompt': 'You classify organization names found in network/WHOIS records into exactly
one of two categories:

- "infra": cloud providers, web hosting companies, CDNs, ISPs, telecoms,
  colocation/datacenter providers, internet registries (e.g. APNIC, RIPE),
  or any organization whose IP address space is used to provide hosting,
  cloud, CDN or connectivity to OTHER companies. Their IP ranges are shared
  across many unrelated end-customers, so a single scanned host cannot be
  attributed to one specific business.
- "end_business": a company that appears to operate in its own industry
  (retail, finance, manufacturing, software product, healthcare, education,
  government, etc.) and whose IP addresses are used for its own operations,
  not resold or hosted for third parties.

Rules:
1. Judge by what the organization's IP address space is used for, not by what the
   organization is best known for. A large technology or retail company that also runs a
   public cloud, hosting or CDN service is "infra", because its address space hosts many
   third parties.
2. If the name alone gives no clear signal (a generic company-style name with no industry
   or provider words), still choose the more likely category but keep confidence at or
   below 0.6. Reserve confidence above 0.85 for names with an unmistakable signal.

Respond with ONLY a JSON object matching this exact schema, no other text:
{"classification": "infra" | "end_business", "confidence": <float 0-1>, "reasoning": "<one short sentence>"}', 'user_prompt': 'Organization name: "Orange S.A."

Classify this organization.'}
response: {"classification": "infra", "confidence": 0.95, "reasoning": "Orange S.A. is a major multinational telecommunications corporation providing internet and network connectivity."}

request:
{'system_prompt': 'You write short, sales-readable risk narratives for a cybersecurity software
sales team. You will be given a numbered list of EVIDENCE items -- real,
structured findings from an external network scan of one business's
internet-facing infrastructure -- plus some basic account metadata.

Rules (do not break these):
1. You may ONLY state facts that appear in the evidence list below. Never
   invent, guess, or embellish a CVE id, port number, product name, or any
   other technical detail that is not explicitly present in the evidence.
2. Every specific technical claim you make in "summary" must be backed by at
   least one evidence item. List the 0-indexed evidence numbers that support
   your narrative in "cited_evidence_indices".
3. Write for a salesperson with no security background: plain language, why
   it matters commercially, no jargon left unexplained.
4. Do not claim or imply any trend over time (e.g. "recently increased",
   "growing exposure") -- this data is a single point-in-time scan snapshot
   with no history to compare against.

Respond with ONLY a JSON object matching this exact schema, no other text:
{"summary": "<2-3 sentence narrative>", "outreach_angle": "<one sentence suggested opening angle for outreach>", "cited_evidence_indices": [<int>, ...]}', 'user_prompt': 'Account: epic.com.mt
Attribution confidence: HIGH
Provider role(s): self_hosted_or_direct
Countries: Malta
Exposure score: 20 (higher = more urgent)
Assets observed: 1

EVIDENCE:
[0] End-of-life software detected: nginx 1.29.1

Write the narrative and outreach angle for this account.'}
response: {"summary":"The scan found that epic.com.mt is running nginx version 1.29.1, which is end‑of‑life software. Because it no longer receives security updates, any newly discovered vulnerabilities will remain unpatched, putting the website and its visitors at risk of compromise.","outreach_angle":"Offer a quick upgrade path to a supported web server version to eliminate exposure from unsupported software.","cited_evidence_indices":[0]}

request:
{'system_prompt': 'You write short internal briefs that help a cybersecurity SALESPERSON decide whether and how
to approach a prospect account. You are given a numbered list of EVIDENCE items -- real
findings from an external network scan of the prospect's internet-facing infrastructure --
plus some basic account metadata.

Rules (do not break these):
1. Facts: state only what the evidence says. Never invent, guess, or embellish a CVE id, port
   number, product name, version, or any other technical detail that is not explicitly in the
   evidence.
2. Citations: list the 0-indexed evidence numbers your summary relies on in
   "cited_evidence_indices". Always include the most severe finding.
3. Perspective: write ABOUT the account in the third person, for the salesperson (for example
   "Acme runs ..." or "The account exposes ..."). Never address the prospect: do not use
   "you" or "your" in the summary. Only "outreach_angle" may be phrased as a question the
   salesperson could ask the prospect.
4. No unsupported consequences: a scan shows exposure, not damage. Do not state or imply that
   data was or will be stolen, lost or leaked, that a breach, ransomware or an attack will or
   can happen, or any business impact. If context helps, add at most ONE short, general,
   hedged sentence about why this type of issue matters (for example "End-of-life software no
   longer receives security patches."), phrased as a property of the issue, not a prediction
   about this account.
5. No trend: this is a single point-in-time scan with no history. Never write "recently",
   "increasing", "growing" or similar.

Respond with ONLY a JSON object matching this exact schema, no other text:
{"summary": "<2-3 sentence third-person brief>", "outreach_angle": "<one sentence suggested opening question for the salesperson to ask>", "cited_evidence_indices": [<int>, ...]}', 'user_prompt': 'Account: myserver.org
Attribution confidence: HIGH
Provider role(s): customer_hosted
Countries: United States
Exposure score: 10 (higher = more urgent)
Assets observed: 1

EVIDENCE:
[0] Self-signed TLS certificate (broken cert hygiene)

Write the narrative and outreach angle for this account.'}

(a hostname or the original text).

The kinds are:
- "components": a technology name detected on a web page (for example "Nginx", "jQuery").
- "cpe": a vendor:product pair (for example "f5:nginx").
- "products": the product name a scanner read from a service banner (for example "Apache httpd").
- "server_headers": the first token of an HTTP Server header (for example "awselb").

- "technology": the canonical, publicly known product name, spelled the way an engineer would write
  it ("Amazon CloudFront", "OpenSSL"). Use null if you do not recognise it.
- "category": exactly one value from allowed_categories.
- "vendor": the company or project that makes it, or null.
- "keep": true if a salesperson could treat it as a meaningful technology the business uses; false

  cannot name, or anything you cannot identify with confidence.

1. Never guess. If you do not clearly recognise a string, set keep to false and technology to null.
   A wrong technology shown to a salesperson is worse than a missing one.
2. If an item is a module or plugin of a larger product, map it to the product a salesperson would
